Ambiguous971 renders · 13 prompts · 2 seeds · pre-registered · 2026-10-05

Does the way a prompt is written change what a block does?

The direction I'm chasing. A knob is useful only if it does the same thing however I happen to write the prompt. My claim: moving the weights gives similar results when the prompt describes the same content; the structure of the text matters less than the content.

What would kill it. A block whose change depends on the wording as much as on the subject, or more than on the seed.

Where we are. The first half holds by eye and by the numbers: rewriting matters about as much as the seed and far less than the subject. The registered verdict is still inconclusive, because a small change of content disturbed a block's effect even less than rewriting did — the opposite of what the design assumed.

In two minutes

Two subjects — an elf brawler in a comic style, a woman asleep in a canoe on a lotus pond — each written four ways with the same facts (original, reordered, a pure tag list, prose with synonyms), plus one version with a single object changed (the elf's gauntlet; the sleeper turned into an old bearded man). Twelve blocks in both directions, two seeds.

The baselines differ from row to row: each writing gives a different pose and framing. The edit does not: under every writing and after the gauntlet change, blk19 + turns the gold pauldron into a straw-like fur, and the antlers shrink or disappear in most frames.

The verdict

By eye the claim holds on every arm: same change across the four writings and after the content change. By the numbers, writing behaves like the seed and the subject dominates. The registered verdict is inconclusive, not supported, because its third condition failed on all twelve arms: changing one object in the prompt disturbed a block's effect less than rewriting it. Stated plainly: the text's structure matters about as much as the seed, less than the subject, and more than a one-object change of content.

Why I might be wrong

  • Two subjects, one seed pair. On the canoe the arms are about half as strong as on the elf, and only 12 of 24 arms are larger than what rewriting alone does to the baseline.
  • The style features are partly sensitive to layout. How close two edits look depends partly on how close the two pictures were to start with; the one-object change kept the layout best, which favours it. This does not explain the subject result.
  • The canoe content change kept two words of the original. The "old bearded man" prompt still reads "one arm bends above her head … across her torso", a leftover of the edit.
  • The eye pass is mine and not blind (page 20).

The data

How it was measured

Each image is reduced to 23 style features; an arm's effect on a prompt is its vector of feature changes from the same prompt's baseline. A is the mean cosine between two such vectors: A_writing across writings of the same subject, A_seed across seeds, A_content_small between the original and the one-object change, A_subject between the two subjects. Only arms whose change is larger than what rewriting does to the baseline (size > 1.15) are scored.

The registered rule

condition needed result
median (A_writing − A_seed) ≥ −0.10 −0.04 met
A_writing > A_subject ≥ 75% of arms 12 of 12 met
A_writing > A_content_small ≥ 60% of arms 0 of 12 not met

Scored arms: blk00 ±, blk09 −, blk12 +, blk13 +, blk15 +, blk17 ±, blk19 +, blk23 +, blk27 ±. On them A_writing runs 0.53–0.92 and A_subject −0.15 to 0.52: what the picture contains decides what a block does to it. A tag list against the original behaves like the other rewrites. The third condition failed because the one-object change kept the picture (layout r of its baseline with the original 0.68–0.76) while rewriting moved pose and framing (0.48–0.76). The design assumed the opposite ordering. The same ordering appears in DINOv2 space (page 25): A_content_small 0.29 > A_seed 0.22 > A_writing 0.16 ≫ A_subject 0.02.

Word order

Before C45, an exploratory bench rendered one prompt in five word orders, two seeds, 56 arms. By eye, blk19 + shrinks or removes the antlers and turns the pauldron to fur in 10 of 10 renders, blk26 + lays the same mosaic of colour cells over the frame in 10 of 10, and blk17 + slims the collar and simplifies the figure in 5 of 5 orders at one seed. With the same features: consistency across orders tracks consistency across seeds (r = 0.92 over 56 arms) and is on average 0.06 higher. Every arm with low consistency is among those whose change is smaller than the reordering itself. The order does change the picture — baselines differ by ΔE 16–31, as much as most edits — but it changes the frame, not the character, and not what a block does to it.

Overturned1619 renders · 46 prompts · 10 seeds · pre-registered · 2026-10-17

What the standard metrics see, and what they miss

The direction I'm chasing. The results on the other pages rest on my eye and on statistics written for this project. A reader will ask what the usual metrics say: image quality, prompt adherence, perceptual distance, content similarity, style descriptors, and visual question answering. I wanted them on the same images, decided before they were computed.

What would kill it. Standard metrics that contradict the published verdicts — or that fail to reproduce the eye's calls when calibrated directly against the visual notes.

Where we are. On the diffusion transformer (962 renders), they confirm the saturation knob against the words and put a price on each preset, but DINOv2 misses cross-prompt family coherence (W = 0.007). On the text encoder (657 renders, C66), 3 of 7 calibration rules pass: VQAScore (clip-flant5-xl) catches lost character traits (pooled AUC = 0.885), and both DINOv2-large and CSD-ViT-L track word-order dispersion (ρ = 0.898 and 0.844) and overall change magnitude (ρ = 0.661 and 0.654). All 4 rules that require separating style from content or measuring cross-character direction coherence fail (T1, T2, T4, T6).

In two minutes

No new renders: first, BRISQUE and CLIP-IQA (quality without a reference), CLIPScore (adherence to the prompt), LPIPS, DISTS and SSIM (distance from the baseline), and DINOv2 cosine (same content as the baseline) were computed on every image of the three confirmatory DiT benches (962 renders) — wording, saturation, prompt family. Second, in C66 (docs/prereg_metric_validation.md), contrastively trained style descriptors (CSD-ViT-L), DINOv2-large, zero-shot CLIP ViT-L/14 genre classification, and VQAScore (clip-flant5-xl) were tested against the pre-existing visual reading notes across 657 text-encoder renders (C64, C65, C72, C74, C75).

Read the figure as two corners. Bottom right: the middle blocks, which move the content most and leave BRISQUE where it was. Top left: the late blocks and the combined preset, which keep the content and raise BRISQUE.

The verdict

On the saturation knob the standard metrics agree with the published verdict: at the same colour gain, block 23 stays closer to the original than the words "colorful" (LPIPS 7 of 7, DINOv2 6 of 7). On the prompt-family presets they put a price on each arm: the late blocks and the combo cost up to +9.6 BRISQUE, the middle blocks nothing measurable, while changing the content most. Across both the DiT and the text encoder, embedding cosine of difference vectors across different subjects (H5 on DINOv2, T1 and T2 on CSD-ViT-L) fails to reproduce what the eye calls "moving in the same stylistic direction." By contrast, within-character distance from baseline (T3 word-order dispersion, T5 change magnitude) and targeted visual question answering (T7 VQAScore for specific character traits, AUC = 0.885) pass their pre-registered thresholds and are cleared for automated evaluation.

Why I might be wrong

  • No-reference quality metrics miss what the eye calls noise. blk26 +0.15 was judged not acceptable in every family by eye and costs +0.4 BRISQUE. A low BRISQUE is not evidence of a clean picture.
  • "No measured cost" is not "no cost". It means these two metrics did not move.
  • The depth-against-cost reading is descriptive. It was pre-specified as a measurement, with no rule that could fail.
  • CLIPScore on the saturation bench is not comparable across conditions. It was computed against each image's own prompt, which for the word conditions includes the added words — a defect of the plan, recorded and not interpreted.
  • Difference-vector cosine confounds magnitude with cross-subject coherence. In T1 (ρ = -0.482), an edit that leaves all 7 characters in their original comic style produces small, noisy residual vectors (low pairwise cosine), whereas a destructive edit (L06, L12) pushes every image far from its baseline along a shared collapse component even when characters land in different visual genres.

The two that do, blk09 + and blk17 +, are also the two that lower adherence most on the blacksmith prompts — where blk09 + turned the woman into a man at one of the two seeds (page 23).

A content embedding does not see it

H5 asked whether the middle blocks' common change, seen by eye inside each family, would show up as coherence of DINOv2-embedding changes. Median within-family coherence of the five middle arms: 0.007 against 0.159 on the style features and a threshold of 0.259. Refuted. In DINOv2 space no arm is family-coherent, late blocks included (all W ≤ 0.06): the same change, "more realistic", points one way for a fox and another way for a car in an embedding built around content.

Wording, in DINOv2 space

A_content_small 0.29 > A_seed 0.22 > A_writing 0.16 ≫ A_subject 0.02: the same ordering as the style features on page 24. The subject dominates; rewriting behaves like the seed.

Calibrating metrics on text-encoder edits

Before using any automatic metric to judge text-encoder experiments (page 30), C66 (docs/prereg_metric_validation.md, docs/metric_validation_result.md) tested four candidate backbones — CSD-ViT-L (contrastive style descriptor, 768-d), DINOv2-large (1024-d), zero-shot CLIP ViT-L/14 (openai), and VQAScore (clip-flant5-xl) — against the human visual reading tables across 657 already-rendered text-encoder images (data/metric_val_images.csv, data/metric_val_tests.csv).

test measure n value rule for validated verdict
T1 Per sheet, median cosine between the 7 characters' CSD change vectors vs "same direction" (yes / partly / no) 34 ρ = -0.482 (p = 0.0039), AUC = 0.056 ρ ≥ 0.40 and AUC ≥ 0.75 not validated
T2 Per character, cosine of its CSD change with the mean change of the other six vs follows / another way 238 AUC = 0.383 AUC ≥ 0.70 not validated
T3 (CSD) Per edit, CSD dispersion across the 5 word orders (minus originals) vs 1–5 visual scores 20 ρ = 0.844 (p = 0.0) ρ ≥ 0.60 validated
T3 (DINOv2) Per edit, DINOv2 dispersion across the 5 word orders vs 1–5 visual scores 20 ρ = 0.898 (p = 0.0) reported reported
T4 CSD distance to baseline, style changed vs unchanged (elf, 55 vs 97) 152 AUC(CSD) = 0.796, AUC(DINOv2) = 0.815 AUC(CSD) ≥ 0.70 and > AUC(DINOv2) not validated
T5 DINOv2 distance to baseline vs ordinal change rating (none … strong, elf) 150 ρ = 0.661 (p = 0.0, ρ_CSD = 0.654) ρ ≥ 0.50 validated
T6 CLIP ViT-L/14 zero-shot top-1 genre vs single genre named in the reading notes 145 accuracy = 0.593, majority = 0.317 accuracy ≥ 0.60 and ≥ 0.467 not validated

Across the seven character traits annotated on the 153 elf images (data/metric_val_vqa.csv), VQAScore (clip-flant5-xl) separates trait loss from retention with a pooled within-trait AUC of 0.885 (data/metric_val_tests.csv):

A likely reason, not tested: text-encoder edits that shift the style also change the character's pose and accessories (page 30), which a content embedding sees. And in T6, zero-shot CLIP ViT-L/14 matched 86 of 145 single-genre notes (0.593, vs 0.317 majority baseline), missing the pre-registered 0.600 threshold (87/145) by a single image (data/metric_val_genre.csv).

Overturned295 renders · 2 prompts · 3 seeds · 2026-10-05

What did not work, and the limits of everything else

The direction I'm chasing. A report that shows only what held invites the reader to wonder what was left out. This page collects the claims this project made and then lost, how they were lost, and what the remaining pages cannot say.

What would kill it. A retraction stated more softly than the claim was, or a limit the other pages hide.

Where we are. Four claims are withdrawn here. Every one of them was made from a statistic and undone by opening the images. That pattern is why every confirmatory page of this report puts the eye pass first.

In two minutes

On 2026-09-28 the analysis of the centre-push bench, written by the assistant I work with, recommended two edits as the best operating points of the project: the macro-block sliders Block_4 and Block_1 pushed to 0.500. Two statistics said they moved the picture far (V, distance from the baseline in units of seed noise) while keeping its line work (L, structure coherence). Nobody had opened those renders. I had been saying the images were breaking; the analysis kept answering with numbers.

Opened at my prompting the next day, both are destroyed. A destroyed picture is far from its baseline, so V is high; and a regular texture is oriented line everywhere, so L is high too. High V with high L meant "destroyed into a regular texture". The bench proposed to push them further was withdrawn.

The verdict

Four claims are overturned: that strong pushes of two macro-blocks keep the drawing; that the structure-coherence statistic can tell damage from steering; that the centre of the stack gives way differently from its ends; and that a CLIP-based delta separates "semantic" from "structural" blocks. The common cause is a statistic read without the images. Every result that survives in this report was scored after an eye pass deposited in advance — which makes that eye, a single observer who knows the conditions, the largest limit of the report.

Why I might be wrong

  • The retractions rest on the same eye whose limits are listed below. For the eye veto, six blind model observers agreed with me on every pair both could resolve.
  • Some of these statistics may be repairable. Structure coherence at a smaller window might flip the two units it gets wrong; that has not been run.
  • The centre-push null concerns macro-blocks, groups of consecutive blocks, not single blocks.

The data

The best doses by the statistic

macro-block, positive V at 0.500 L at 0.500 what the render shows
Block_4 3.28 1.204 no subject; crumpled-paper texture of dense black strokes
Block_1 3.84 1.058 no subject; colour confetti

Arm means over prompts and seeds (docs/centre_push_result.md §4); the figure shows the unit means of one prompt (data/centre_push_units.csv). At 0.350, Block_4 + already flattens faces into masks; Block_1 + at 0.350 on this prompt and seed keeps the blacksmith intact, framed closer. The retraction is in docs/centre_push_result.md §4, where the original table is kept and struck through.

A measure with the sign wrong

The centre-push bench had a pre-registered eye veto: twelve pairs of renders, and for each I said which was more broken. I resolved 9 and agreed with L on 7, below the registered 8 of 12, so the label "L not validated by eye" applies. Seven of nine is not a rout. The rout is in the two disagreements: both are Block_6 + 0.080, which L scores above its own baseline and which I, and six blind model observers in both orientations of the sheets, call broken. Block_1 − 0.500 is the same case (L 1.02–1.03, broken in both pairs). A statistic that says a picture gained structure on the condition three independent looks call damaged has the sign wrong.

The centre is not special

The bench's primary asked whether the four central macro-blocks give way under a push differently from the two at the ends. T = +0.053, p = 0.19; the range guard passed, so this is a null. Block_5, in the centre, gives way hardest of all; Block_1, at an end, less than five of the eight central arms. A post hoc reclassification of Block_5 as an end gives p = 0.02 and is recorded as such, not as the verdict. The single-block map on page 21 shows why macro-blocks were the wrong unit: they cut across the groups that push together.

Semantic routing

An analysis written by another assistant, never published, ranked 56 single-block arms by the difference between how consistent an arm's CLIP-embedding change is across ten images of one prompt and across 26 images of different prompts, and read a large difference as a "semantic router". The audit (docs/semantic_routing_audit.md) found:

  • no script in the repository computes the p-values it quotes, and its survivor count is 12 in the text and 16 in the summary;
  • doses are not part of the key, so different doses of one arm are mixed or silently dropped;
  • the difference measures how alike the images are: ten renders of one character against 26 different scenes; every visible edit is expected to score positive;
  • its second-ranked "semantic router", blk26 +, lays the same mosaic of colour cells over any content, white background included — the least semantic effect in the set.

What survives is each column on its own: for a fixed content most arms move the CLIP embedding the same way whatever the word order (page 24), and the arms most stable across 26 different scenes are grain, blur and texture.

What the numbers could not see

Notebook page 11 records three more cases. Five conditions recommended from displacement statistics ranked 75th to 80th of 80 on structure coherence; the condition picked by eye ranked 12th. An edit removed all colour from a leaf while leaving the leaf intact, in 9 of 20 fresh seeds and 0 of 20 controls, and never when the prompt named a colour — an open lead on which colours an edit can reach. A generality test for that effect was run on subjects whose colour was never in doubt, so its null meant nothing.

The style-direction result of notebook page 09 is also overturned; it is discussed beside the result it seems to contradict, on page 23.

Lessons kept as rules

  • No sentence about how a render looks without opening it at 1:1. When the eye and a statistic disagree, the statistic is the suspect (pitfall 90).
  • A distance from the baseline cannot tell steering from damage. A destroyed image is far.
  • Before claiming that something has not been done, search for it (pitfalls 87, 88).
  • Before fixing a threshold on the agreement of two measured things, measure how well each agrees with itself (pitfall 89).

Limits of this report

  • One model. Krea-2 only; whether any of this transfers to another architecture is untested.
  • One observer, who knows the conditions. Every eye pass is mine; hashed names do not blind me (page 20). All images are published so that the eye pass can be repeated.
  • Small confirmatory samples. 16 to 40 cells per test; seven cells for the matched comparison of page 22.
  • Doses calibrated on single images. Some are too strong for a preset (page 23).
  • The guide to each block on page 21 is provisional. One observer, a few prompts, one dose per direction; most of its Style-band entries are unmeasured and it is meant to be expanded.
  • One test is inconclusive by its own rule (page 24); the weights result is marginal (page 21); the middle blocks' coherence is seen by eye only (pages 23, 25).
  • Not run: a forward-pass measurement of each block's write into the residual stream; a clean-up pass after a preset; the character-consistency test proposed on page 23.

Ambiguous1730 renders · 54 prompts · 2026-10-05

Appendix A: other kinds of edit

The direction I'm chasing. Before single blocks, this project edited the weights in other ways: reordering whole blocks inside the checkpoint, permuting them, scrambling signs. Some of those results passed pre-registered tests, and one produced an observation worth keeping.

What would kill it. Nothing new is tested here. The appendix only reports, with their status, results that live in the exploratory notebook.

Where we are. Two pre-registered results hold for block reordering. One observation — attributes appearing that the model normally leaves out — is kept as a curiosity, with its weaknesses stated.

In two minutes

These edits are not single-block scaling. A block derangement swaps the weights of whole blocks with one another, scaled by a dose; a permutation reorders them; a sign scramble flips signs so that the weights move exactly as far without any structure. They are reported here because two of their results are pre-registered and replicated, and because one of them tells something about what a weight edit can bring into a picture. The full pages, with figures, data and reproducibility blocks, are in the exploratory notebook.

The verdict

Block derangement has two confirmed effects: the sign of the edit decides whether hatching strokes cross or run parallel (16 of 16 prompts), and the edit enlarges the subject in the frame (9 of 10 new styles). A permutation brought out an attribute the prompt asked for and the model usually leaves out, in 19 of 20 seeds; it is an observation, not a result, and is boxed as such below.

Why I might be wrong

  • These are a different family of edits from the rest of the report. Nothing here says anything about single blocks.
  • The hatching measure was not checked against the calibrated preset, which moves it the other way; for that preset the measure may not track hatching at all (notebook page 06).
  • The enlargement may be a matter of size, not structure. The scramble at equal distance was not rendered.
  • The attribute observation was scored by me, with the condition visible, on one prompt family.

The data

The hatching axis

In a comic-style corpus, block derangement pushed positive crossed the hatching strokes and pushed negative ran them parallel. A pre-registered test on 16 new prompts confirmed the sign: crosshatch entropy +0.288, 16 of 16 prompts, 79 of 80 pairs. The same test overturned the third family of the prediction — the sign scramble's exploratory effect did not come back (5 of 16 prompts). Full page: notebook page 06.

The subject grows

Pre-registered on ten styles that did not exist when the prediction was frozen: under block derangement at double dose the subject's area grows by a geometric mean of 1.234, in 9 of 10 styles, with all three predicted signs correct. The same round measured the blinding of the eye pass and found it failed (page 20). Full page: notebook page 03.

A curiosity: attributes that appear

Observed, not established. A prompt asked for "small barnacle-like clusters studding one earlobe". The stock model drew them in 1 of 20 seeds; a block permutation drew them in 19 of 20; a sign scramble moving the weights exactly as far (D = 0.0538) drew them in 1 of 20. On a separate corpus — a rally car in a jungle, eight drawing styles, no lights named in the prompt — lit headlights went from 10 of 35 at baseline to 31 of 38 under one edit and to 0 of 39 under another.

Its weaknesses. A different kind of edit from the rest of this report. The barnacle round was scored by me with the condition visible. The headlights were scored blind, but on the very renders that produced the observation; the exact test is at its floor (p = 0.031, Holm 0.19). The pre-registered confirmation on a second corpus could not decide anything: 9 of its 10 prompts never lit a headlight in any condition. One prompt family; the test of generality was designed and never run.

What makes it worth keeping is the control: the same distance in weight space, without structure, does nothing. How the weights move mattered, not how far. Full page: notebook page 02.

Holds514 renders · 7 prompts · 6 seeds · pre-registered · 2026-10-05

A preset made by eye, tested blind on characters it never saw

The direction I'm chasing. The block map is only useful if someone can use it: look at what each block does, mix a few of them into a preset of their own, and get the look they had in mind — on new pictures, not only on the ones they tuned it on. And the character has to stay the same character.

What would kill it. A preset that only works on the pictures it was tuned on; a look that someone who does not know which image carries it cannot pick out; a face that changes into someone else.

Where we are. The look carries over to characters the preset never saw, and a blind observer picked it 56 times out of 56. The character stays recognisable, but the face moves a little more than a change of seed moves it, and an expression can go flat. The test had one observer and no sheets with two different characters.

In two minutes

Seven character portraits written in one template ("Western comics style, close-up portrait, frontal view.", then the character). On four of them I looked at every single block pushed both ways (457 renders) and wrote a preset by eye: ten blocks, doses between 0.05 and 0.35. What I wanted, in my words before any test: a more American-comic look leaning toward animation: flat colours and clean lines, with proportions exaggerated only slightly compared with the default. The preset was frozen, the rules and scoring code committed, and only then were all seven characters rendered at four new seeds, with and without it.

The three columns marked new are the test: the halfling, the dragonborn and the tiefling were written into the plan but never rendered while I was tuning. Then someone who had never seen the project looked at the pairs without knowing which side carried the preset.

The verdict

A preset written by eye from the single-block map transfers: its change is as coherent on three unseen characters as on the four it was tuned on (0.51 against 0.61), and a blind observer chose it as the closer match to the described look in 56 of 56 comparisons. The characters stay themselves — far closer to their own base than to any other character — but the rule I set for the face, "no more change than a new seed", was not met. Looking at the worst cases, the preset can also turn a prompted expression flat and remove small prompted details.

Why I might be wrong

  • One blind observer, and close to me. My partner, who had not seen the project and did not know which image carried the preset or what result was expected; I was out of the room. Her answers are strong evidence that the change is visible and goes the described way, not a measure of how many people would agree.
  • The question named the look. She was asked which image matched "more American comic / animation", not to describe what changed. A preset that only did something else would have failed; a preset that did this plus something unwanted could still pass.
  • "Same character" had no foil. Every sheet showed one character twice, so answering yes every time could not be wrong. The evidence on identity is ArcFace, not the observer.
  • The model observers did not work. The pre-registered first blind protocol used three model instances; the first read position, not pictures (LEFT on 51 of 56 sheets), and the other two were not run. That arm is reported as not completed.
  • My own eye pass is not blind (page 20). It said yes to every question, which is why the blind test was added.
  • Seven characters in one drawn style, one preset, four seeds. Nothing here says how a preset for photographs would fare.

The data

The look carries over

Coherence is the agreement between the changes the preset makes on two pictures, measured on 23 style statistics (page 20): 1 means the same change, 0 unrelated. The rules, written before the test renders:

rule threshold result verdict
G_S the preset agrees with itself across seeds median ≥ 0.50 0.78 pass
H1 coherent across the three new characters median ≥ 0.40 0.51 supported
H2 no worse than on the four calibration characters ≥ 0.61 − 0.15 0.51 supported

Data: data/portrait_preset_tests.csv, data/portrait_preset_measures.csv, data/portrait_preset_style_features.csv. The reproduction check opened the batch: a phase A base, rendered again, is the same file pixel for pixel (largest difference 0); all 57 planned renders are present.

A blind observer

Each sheet showed the base and the preset of one character at one seed, side by side, under a random number; every pair appeared twice, once with the sides swapped, in a shuffled order of 56. The key was committed before anyone answered.

original set mirrored set verdict
position check: same side named on both versions of a pair 0 of 28 pass
H4 preset chosen, held-out characters 12/12 (p = 0.0002) 12/12 supported
H5 "same character", held-out characters 12/12 12/12 passes, without foils
calibration characters, preset chosen (reported) 16/16 16/16

Answers: data/portrait_preset_blind_answers_human.csv; key: data/portrait_preset_blind_key.csv; tally: data/portrait_preset_blind_tests_human.csv. The model observer's answers and diagnostic tally are in data/portrait_preset_blind_answers_model_obs1.csv and data/portrait_preset_blind_tests_model_obs1_diagnostic.csv.

The face

ArcFace, a face-recognition network, gives one vector per detected face; two faces of the same person score high. It found no face in three of the four gnome preset images and in two tiefling images, one of them a base, so the identity rule was scored on the halfling and the dragonborn:

character base vs preset, same seed base vs base, another seed rule: first above second
halfling (new) 0.75 0.82 no
dragonborn (new) 0.74 0.75 no

H3 is refuted. The calibration characters show the same pattern. Described after the test, over every detected face: the same character at another seed 0.80 (39 pairs), base against preset 0.74 (23), two different characters 0.29 (312, highest 0.68). The preset keeps each face far closer to itself than to anyone else, and a little further than a seed change does — and these prompts are so specific that a seed change barely moves the face. Data: data/portrait_preset_faces.csv.

What the preset takes away

After every number was in, I opened at 1:1 the seven pairs ArcFace marked worst — the gnome at three seeds, the tiefling at two, the half-orc and the dwarf at one. Not blind, and selected.

  • No deformation in any of the seven; the lost detections on the gnome are not damage. Glasses, ears, beard and robe on the gnome, horns, scarf and yellow jacket on the tiefling: each pair is the same character.
  • Small prompted details go with the hatching: the half-orc's dirt smudges across the nose, the gnome's glowing chalk dust, the tiefling's embroidered coat. "Clean lines" also means fewer small marks, including requested ones.
  • Prompted shapes can drift. The tiefling is prompted with "short curling horns swept flat against cropped silver hair" and a "yellow fancy jacket"; at all four seeds the preset makes the horns larger and heavier and the jacket plain:

  • Expressions can go flat. The gnome is prompted "wide-eyed manic curiosity": wide-eyed and mild in all three bases, frowning in all three presets. The half-orc's "fierce defiant snarl" becomes a closed, stern face — the largest drift of the seven, and its lowest ArcFace score.

The preset contains block 8 at +0.15, which my own guide on page 21 lists as giving less expression; it is the first suspect, and scaling it alone on these portraits would test it. Details: docs/portrait_preset_result.md.

Holds2120 renders · 7 prompts · 10 seeds · pre-registered · 2026-10-08

Inside a block — attention, MLP, and what an edit costs

The direction I'm chasing. Every block of Krea-2 has two halves, an attention and an MLP, and until now we had only ever scaled them together. If the knobs live at a finer grain than the block, the halves should do different things, and the noise that comes with a push might belong to one of them.

What would kill it. The two halves doing the same thing, or the noise following the dose rather than the half; and, for the practical claim, middle-block edits costing as much as late ones once they are tried on pictures they were not chosen on.

Where we are. The halves differ, and an eye blind to the condition puts the noise mostly in the MLP. Middle-block edits reshape a drawing and spare its surface far more than late ones do, pre-registered on new prompts. But they are not free: a few of them pay on new pictures.

In two minutes

Each block of the model has an attention part (five matrices) and an MLP part (three). An atlas (C59) scaled each half alone, in both directions, for all 28 blocks, on three prompts and three seeds: 1016 renders. The person who knows the images best then labelled every block, half and direction blind, choosing among nine kinds of artefact and three strengths.

Noise lives mostly in the MLP. The attention joins it only in the last three blocks. The first block is the strangest: either half alone wrecks the picture, while both together keep its composition.

The labels also showed that the edits praised as "good for the comic" were the ones that changed the picture most, and they sat in the middle of the stack. A pre-registered test on new prompts and seeds (C60) confirmed it: middle-block edits change more and damage less. They still cost something, in four of ten edits.

A third test (C61) tried to overturn the older claim that every push costs fine texture. It could not: on its own comic prompts the old numbers came back almost to the third decimal.

The verdict

Holds for the practical claim, pre-registered (C60): on comic and cartoon prompts, edits to blocks 1-19 change the picture more than edits to blocks 20-27 and damage its surface in 19% of pairs against 79%. Holds that this is not free either: by the rule fixed before the labels, the middle edits carry a detectable cost. Open for where the noise sits (blind, but without a decision rule) and for the first block. Ambiguous for the cost of a push: page 05 replicates on its own prompts, the test as a whole did not decide.

Why I might be wrong

One observer. Every eye label is mine. I was blind to the condition, and my self-agreement on the damage threshold was 1.00 on the 15 repeats of C60, but my eye is also the one that chose the middle-block edits in C59. New prompts and seeds guard against fitting the images, not against fitting a taste.

"Slight" does not reproduce. In both eye passes every disagreement between a first and a repeated showing was "slight" against "none". Only medium and stronger count as damage here.

The measures do not see the noise. The fine-texture measure of page 05, the noise estimator of C58 and a band-pass measure all failed against the eye on the noise that matters. As a size of change, the same measures rank the eye's noise only moderately (AUC 0.75-0.81). A pre-registered search for a better one (C62, eight candidates chosen on C59 and tested on C60) found none: the best remained the size of the fine-texture change, AUC 0.79 on the test set, below its 0.85 bar (docs/noise_metric_result.md). Every noise statement on this page rests on the eye.

One dose, illustration-heavy. All tests use ±0.35, except C61 at ±0.20. Six of seven prompts are drawn; the only photographs are in C61, where they behaved differently.

The data

Where the noise sits

The split atlas pushed the attention (wq, wk, wv, gate, wo) or the MLP (gate, up, down) of one block by ±0.35, through granular_json. Both checks passed to the pixel: the atlas baseline reproduced, and all eight matrices through the granular path equalled the whole block through the vector. I labelled 168 sheets at seed 2718281, one per block, half and sign, each showing the same edit on the three prompts, plus 20 unannounced repeats.

68 of 168 sheets carry an artefact and 46 carry noise (blotches, grain, collapse or a regular screen). Blocks 2, 3, 5 and 7 to 9 are clean in all six conditions. Among the 19 block-sign cells where either half is noisy, the MLP is noisier in 13, the attention in 2, with 4 ties. At blocks 26 and 27 pushed positive both halves are noisy and the whole block is worse than either. A first reading of mine from small thumbnails had put the block-26 noise in the attention alone; at full resolution both halves carry it, and that reading was withdrawn (docs/split_atlas_eye_result.md).

The first block

At -0.35 the attention alone posterises every picture into flat saturated colour, and on the rally into a mosaic. The MLP alone replaces the subject. Both happen in 9 of 9 cells. Lowered together, the composition holds (layout r 0.69-0.80), but at full resolution the surface is covered in blotches. The two halves compensate each other for content, not for texture.

The damage also changes kind. Unbalanced, the block breaks the picture at the level of content and colour: the attention alone pushes chroma up by 13 to 68 points and streaks the surface with rainbow fringes, the MLP alone smooths it into a painted, screen-textured surface and replaces the subject. Balanced, it keeps the content and the colour (chroma within 2 points) and pays in blotches. One way to read it, not tested: in the first block the two halves write large, partly opposite contributions, so lowering one alone leaves the other uncompensated, while lowering both keeps the balance but thins the fine detail the block adds.

Searched across the whole atlas (seed 2718281, where the whole block exists), this is unique to the first block lowered: in 3 of 3 prompts there, and in only 5 other cells of the remaining 165. Everywhere else the rule runs the other way: in 125 of 168 cells the whole block changes the composition more than either half alone. Block 0 raised does not compensate either. A milder echo exists for colour at block 24 raised, where the attention adds chroma (+2.1) and the MLP removes it (−1.6) and the whole block moves it little (−0.2).

Form against surface

The labels suggested, after the fact, that the sheets praised for the comic changed the picture more than the noisy ones (layout r 0.74 against 0.87). C60 tested it on three new prompts (two comics, one cartoon) and three new seeds. It used ten middle-block edits chosen by rule, the praised sheets, and ten late-block edits drawn at random from the noisy ones. 191 renders; 180 blind pairs of edit and baseline with the side random, plus 15 repeats.

middle edits (blocks 1-19) late edits (blocks 20-27) test
layout r with the baseline, median per edit 0.721 0.837 p = 0.007
change seen by eye, 0-2 1.59 0.47 p = 0.0002
damage medium or stronger, edited side 17 / 90 71 / 90 baseline sides 0 / 180

A preference question was dropped before any label, at my request, as too subjective.

What the middle costs

The middle edits are not free. By the rule fixed before the labels, a cost is present: 0.19 against 0, Newcombe 95% [0.11, 0.28]. It sits in four edits, all at medium: block 19 MLP + in 8 of 9 pairs, block 1 attention + and block 17 whole + in 4 of 9, block 13 whole - in 1 of 9. Six edits are at 0 of 9. At 100% the damage is not the late blocks' grain: flat areas such as a sky break into patches or rectangles. Block 19 MLP + was clean on the prompts it was chosen on and is the most damaged here, so the cost depends on the prompt.

A follow-up (C63, docs/clean_six_result.md) put the six edits that came out clean on four new illustration prompts at three new seeds, 72 blind pairs, with two late-block edits as a positive control (damaged in 24 of 24). Four of the 72 were damaged against none of their baselines, three of them from block 9 attention +: too few pairs to call the six free (the interval reaches 13%) or costly (it reaches below zero). Block 2 whole −, block 8 MLP +, block 9 whole + and block 18 MLP − are at 0 of 21 damaged pairs across the two tests.

The cost of a push, revisited

Notebook page 05 found, pre-registered, that pushing any block costs fine texture, more toward the output. C61 tried to overturn the general wording. It pushed every whole block by ±0.20, page 05's dose and path, on its two comic prompts and two photographs, at four new seeds: 913 renders. The first render matched page 05's own file to the pixel. By its own rules the test decided nothing. The gate, which required the bench to see the late-block cost, failed (0.989, p = 0.26). The primary, blocks 1-22, was undecided (0.996, 95% [0.981, 1.011]).

The figure shows why. On the comic prompts both of page 05's numbers come back: 0.989 for blocks 1-22 and 0.934 for 23-27, against 0.989 and 0.932. On the photographs the last blocks add high frequency instead (block 27: 1.27), which this measure counts as a gain. Page 05 stands on its own ground, and its "any block" is untested beyond it. Including block 27 in the gate, a block page 05 itself called an outlier, was a weakness of the design.

Holds1917 renders · 74 prompts · 8 seeds · pre-registered · 2026-10-18

The text encoder — how hard it pushes, and where the picture goes

The direction I'm chasing. Krea-2 reads the prompt with a language model, Qwen3-VL-4B, before the image model draws anything. If the same weight edits that work on the image model work on that text encoder, they might change what the picture is about — the genre, the style — rather than its surface. And once the picture changes, I want to know why it goes where it goes.

What would kill it. Edits whose effect cannot be predicted from anything we can measure on the text side; and, for the "why", an explanation that does not survive a test fixed before the data.

Where we are. How much a picture changes is predictable from the text side alone, mostly by the kind of edit. Where it goes is now clearer: anime is this character's fallback when the style words stop working, shown directly by removing them — but only for the elf: other characters fall back to painting or realistic renders. Random pushes reach that fallback only if they vary from token to token, and each real edit has a direction of its own: one protects the comic, another drives it to anime. Why a given edit points where it does is still open. And a dose ladder showed that the full-strength edits do not break the picture: the style holds up to about d = 0.70, and before it moves, the edit has often already changed who is drawn. Blind labels by two people confirm it: two of the edits cost the character far more than random pushes of the same size, and turn dark skin lighter. Since then I've looked inside: one layer, L06, writes almost all of the encoder's internal signal; the damage does not travel through the readings right after the edited layer, and the two halves of the readings together fall short of the full edit. Switching off half of the very first layer makes the picture write the prompt. And on the prompt itself, the separators make no difference, while BREAK breaks the scene.

In two minutes

Before the image model draws, a language model reads the prompt and hands over a long list of numbers, the conditioning. That's all the image model will ever know about your words. So I edited that language model the same way I edit the image model: one layer, its attention or its MLP, zeroed or doubled.

The pictures change a lot, and in a particular way. They do not get noisy, as they do when the image model is pushed hard. They change genre — a Western comic becomes anime or a cartoon — and usually who is drawn: the character loses her antlers, her ears, her skin tone, often her identity. The same edit on the same words in a different order can land in a different genre.

The useful part: how much a picture changes can be predicted without rendering it. Measure how far the edit moves the conditioning, and you know roughly how far the picture will move. That held in two tests fixed in advance — but mostly because it tells kinds of edit apart. Among the edits that change genre, all of them large, it says little about which change more.

The puzzle: where the picture goes. When the elf changes genre, she goes to anime in 39 of 50 cases. I tested two explanations. Maybe the picture stops paying attention to the words "western comics": no. Maybe the edit pushes the text the way writing "anime" would: no, the push points somewhere else entirely, and it is 5 to 24 times larger than swapping a style word.

Then I stopped guessing and looked at the fallback directly. Remove the three style words and the elf is drawn as anime, every time. Anime is where this description goes when nothing holds it in a style. Seven other characters, stripped of their style words, fall back to painting or realistic renders instead: there is no single default.

Random pushes as large as the edits, with no weight touched, also reach it, but only when they vary from token to token: the same random vector added to every token changes nothing. And the real edits are not random: the edit with the largest push keeps the comic every time, while random pushes of its size break it almost every time.

Last, I asked whether those edits were simply too strong. I rendered three of them at twelve doses, from a tenth of the edit to the full one. Nothing changes style below 0.70, and no picture breaks, even at full dose. But the character goes first. The half-orc stops looking like a half-orc — pointed ears, grey skin, undercut and warrior knot go — while she is still drawn as a comic; the style changes only later. For me this is the real damage: the edit makes the model forget what I asked for, and it fills the gap with a more generic person.

So I measured it blind: a yes/no question for every trait in the prompt, one question at a time, with no dose or edit shown. The traits fall steadily with the dose, and they go before the style. Then the control: random pushes of the same size. Someone else labelled those, without knowing anything about the study. Random pushes keep nine traits in ten; L06 and L14 keep half to two thirds. And when the skin changes under those two edits, it becomes lighter, every time; under random pushes it almost never changes. The prompts never name a skin tone: the edit takes away what holds the character, and the model fills the gap with its default.

Then I opened the text encoder itself. A probe that only reads, run on all 36 layers, shows one layer doing almost all the writing: the MLP of layer 6 takes the internal signal from about 400 to about 13,100, and every layer after it, up to 33, adds a few percent. And L06 doubled is the edit that turned my portraits into photographs. That is a coincidence worth testing, not an explanation yet.

The image model doesn't read only the encoder's last layer: it takes twelve readings of every word, at layers 2, 5, 8 and so on up to 35, and mixes them. So I asked which readings carry the damage. I let the L06 and L14 edits reach only some readings and kept the others at their original value. The readings right after the edited layer do nothing. The early and middle ones cost more traits than the late ones, in five of six cases, but by a margin just short of the bar I had fixed (0.146 against 0.15). And the strangest part: the two halves together don't add up to the full edit. Under L14 they cost less than half of what the whole edit costs; the whole edit changes the person every time, the halves never.

Then two curiosities. Switch off half of the encoder's first layer and the image model stops drawing: it writes, filling the picture with fragments of the prompt ("realist: om wetern comips"). Switch off the whole layer and you get coloured noise, no text at all. Measured on the encoder side, half a layer keeps the words recognisable at a normal size; the whole layer gone loses both.

And people asked me about punctuation. On two complex prompts with four characters each, commas, periods, semicolons, no punctuation at all, or no "Character 1 (…)" labels: no difference, within a quarter of an error. BREAK, the old trick from CLIP-based models to stop concepts bleeding, does the opposite here: it breaks the scene in 16 of 16 pairs.

The verdict

Holds, pre-registered twice: the size of the push on the conditioning predicts how much the picture changes (Spearman 0.71 and 0.80), mostly between kinds of edit; within the edits that change genre it nearly vanishes (exploratory). Holds: the push is shared by the whole prompt plus small regions of 2-4 tokens bounded by commas. Holds: these edits change genre and identity, with less surface-quality loss than a DiT preset. Overturned: one edit moving different characters the same way; the genre switch coming from less attention on the style words; the switch coming from a text-like push toward "anime". Holds, pre-registered (C72): without its style words the elf is drawn as anime. Holds (C73): each character has its own fallback, mostly painting or realistic. Overturned (C73): strong edits send a character to its own fallback. Ambiguous: whether random pushes of the same size reach the fallback as often as edits — yes if they vary across tokens, no if they are one shared vector. Open: that each edit's own direction decides; what single phrases draw alone; anime as the usual destination of a switch. Ambiguous: whether the strong edits separate word orders inside the image model. Holds (C74): along a dose ladder the pictures move toward the full-dose picture, and the style changes before coherence breaks, which it never does. Holds* (C74): the change is gradual, by the rule fixed in advance; *but only pooled: L14 slides, L06 jumps. Holds (C75): the first cost of L06 and L14 is the character, before the style; the cost depends on the edit's direction, not its size (random pushes of the same size keep the character, and L28 keeps it better than they do); under L06 and L14 dark skin turns lighter. Ambiguous (C75): that L28 costs traits without changing style. Holds (C78): separators make no difference on complex prompts; BREAK breaks the scene. Open (C77): half of layer 0 switched off makes the picture write the prompt (4 of 6, bar 5). Open, described: L06's MLP writes almost all of the encoder's internal signal. Holds (C79): the damage does not travel through the readings right after the edited layer. Ambiguous (C79): that it travels through the early and middle readings rather than the late ones (+0.146 against a bar of +0.15).

Why I might be wrong

One observer, not blind. Every genre and intensity label is mine. On the order grids I saw the edit names, and I had seen these pictures before. I gave the intensity labels after I knew the first test had failed.

One prompt carries the word-order story. C69, C70 and C71 rest on the elf in five word orders at one seed. The anime default may be specific to this prompt or this character.

The fallback rests on one character. Anime is the fallback of this elf description; C73 confirmed that other characters fall back elsewhere. In the no-style pictures the character, pose and composition stay; what changes is the rendering — flatter cel shading, no hatching — and the label "anime" is my reading of that change.

Genre labels hide sub-styles, and the doses are extreme. While labelling I noticed that each label covers very different sub-styles: two pictures labelled "Western comic" can look nothing alike, so "no switch" does not mean "same style". All these edits zero or double a layer half; at that strength part of what is labelled a change of genre may be a loss of stylistic coherence. C74 checked this with a dose ladder and comparative judgements: no picture lost coherence, up to full dose. The labels of sub-style remain mine.

Size mostly sorts kinds of edit. The two tests of the size of the push were fixed on all edits together. Checked afterwards within one kind, the relation nearly vanishes for the MLP-doubled edits — the ones that change genre — and holds at 0.46-0.66 for the others (data/te_size_within_type.csv). Part of that may be a ceiling: 28 of the 35 MLP-doubled edits were already labelled strong.

Mostly large doses. Almost everything here is at ±1: a layer half doubled or removed. C74 adds twelve doses, but for three edits, three characters and two seeds only.

Traits are judgements too. C75 fixed the list of traits before any label and asked them blind, but some are judgements of degree (age, androgyny, "reads as a dwarf"), and those are where the two labellers disagree most. The part B2 set was shortened after I had seen part A (every cell at full dose, half at 0.70 and half at 0.85), and two questions were reworded for the second labeller, so on those two our answers are not compared. Three characters, two seeds, one kind of edit. In C74, one row has an onset of "never" although the picture changes at 0.80 (I checked); it is kept as downloaded and changes no verdict.

What the measures do not see. The conditioning is what the image model receives, not what it does with it. Attention says where a phrase is read, not what it says. C71 averages over all the tokens of a prompt, which can hide an effect concentrated on a few words.

The newest results are thin. C77 is one seed, four prompts and my own reading of the pictures. C78 rests on two prompts that I wrote, and most questions sit near the ceiling, so a small effect of punctuation cannot be excluded. In C79 I labelled alone, and contact sheets showing the conditions existed before I labelled: my perfect agreement with myself on repeats (kappa 1.00) says I was consistent, not that I was not influenced. The probe of the 36 layers is a description: no prediction was fixed before it.

The intensity scale mixed two things. On L28 MLP doubled, all five pictures are labelled Western comic but intensity 3, "entirely another genre". Opened next to the original, they stay comics with a very different rendering. In practice intensity measured the overall change of style.

The data

The size of the push

C67 encoded the elf prompt under every edit of the C64 pilot (721 encodes, no images) and measured, for every token and every reading the edit can reach, how far the conditioning moved. Doubling an MLP moves it most (median 0.89), then doubling an attention (0.29), removing an MLP (0.18) and removing an attention (0.11) — the same order in which the eye ranked the pictures. Scaling only the queries and keys of a layer changes nothing the image model receives: a normalisation inside the attention cancels it.

test value rule verdict
C67 E1 — size against "how much it changed", 140 elf edits Spearman 0.71; AUC 0.80 for style changed ≥ 0.50 supported
C70 G3 — size against the rate of genre switches, 20 edits Spearman 0.73 ≥ 0.50 supported
C70 G3d — size against the mean intensity 0-3, 20 edits Spearman 0.80 ≥ 0.50 supported

These tests pooled every kind of edit, and the kinds differ a lot in size. Within one kind the picture is different (exploratory, data/te_size_within_type.csv): attention doubled 0.66, MLP zeroed 0.65, attention zeroed 0.46 on the C67 material, but MLP doubled 0.06 (n 35). On the C70 material the MLP-doubled edits give 0.36 (n 11, p 0.28). So the size of the push tells a strong kind of edit from a mild one; among the strong ones, the ones that change genre, it does not say which changes the picture more.

A shared push made of small regions

An exploratory analysis of C67 found that each edit pushes the conditioning of very different prompts in nearly the same direction (cosine 0.91-0.99 between prompts, 0.55 between different edits). C68 took away that shared push and looked at what was left. Two neighbouring tokens are pushed in related directions; four or five tokens apart the relation has halved (half-life 3 tokens). Groups follow the commas, most clearly in the middle of the encoder. These regions are as stable across word orders as the shared push, so they do not explain why word order matters (C68 H3, Spearman -0.37, not supported).

Genre and identity, not surface

The C64 pilot doubled or removed each half of each of the 35 layers the image model reads, on the elf, and I labelled every picture blind (140 edits, 10 repeats). Doubling changes far more than removing: strong changes in 40 of 70 against 4 of 70. Surface damage is rare (medium or strong in 8 of 140). My notes describe genres more often than noise: anime, chibi, a 1990s cartoon, children's illustration. C65 confirmed the quality side on seven characters: BRISQUE improves slightly (-1.52) where the DiT preset of page 28 costs +8.09.

This agrees with what others found on Stable Diffusion: a targeted edit of one MLP matrix of the CLIP text encoder changes what the model draws with image quality (FID) nearly unchanged, while the same kind of update made in the image model's cross-attention sometimes leaves the pictures incoherent (README, ref. 30). Their edits are aimed at one concept and built not to disturb the rest; mine scale a whole layer, and still cost little surface. Neither study compares the two halves at the same size of change: that is roadmap item C86.

No common direction across characters

C65 applied 20 edits chosen from the pilot to seven fantasy characters at two seeds. A DiT preset moves them the same way (page 28); these edits do not. Only 4 of 20 were coherent across characters (the bar was 14). The eye and the statistics disagreed in a telling way: the strong edits shift every picture the same way in colour and contrast, but each character lands in a different genre. At ±1 these edits also change who is drawn: identity is kept for at most two eligible characters in 19 of 20 edits.

The figure also shows that the destination depends on the character. On these portraits L06 MLP doubled turns the dwarf and the gnome into photographs, not anime; on the elf (below) the same edit scatters the word orders between comic, anime and cartoon. Anime is the elf's fallback, not every character's.

Where the switches go

In C70 I named the genre of each of the 105 pictures of the word-order test (seed 3141592) and, separately, how far each one moved from its original (0-3). The five originals are all Western comic, so word order alone does not change the genre. Of the 100 edited pictures, 50 changed genre: 39 to anime, 11 to cartoon, none to realistic or painting. No edit that zeroes a layer half changed the genre. Two patterns appear among those that do. L05, L20 and L25 MLP doubled send all five orders to anime. L06, L09, L12 and L14 MLP doubled scatter them across genres; these are the edits he had scored highest for word-order dependence.

Inside the image model

C69 re-rendered 25 pictures — the elf in five orders, the original and four edits — with a probe that only reads the image model's attention. All 25 came out identical to the originals, pixel for pixel. At every step and in every block, the probe recorded where each part of the picture looks among the phrases of the prompt.

The strong edits move these maps about twice as much as the mild ones (P4: 0.29 and 0.30 against 0.16 and 0.13). Whether they also make the five orders read the prompt in more different places is not settled. P1 passed by a margin of 0.003, carried by L12 alone; L06 does not do it, though its pictures diverge as much. The blocks where L12 raises the divergence most are 12, 25, 18, 15 and 16.

Not less attention on the style words

The first explanation for the genre switch: weaken the words that name the style, and the model's own taste takes over. L06 MLP doubled does cut the attention on the three style phrases, from 0.095 to 0.054 of all attention on text, in every order. But L12 MLP doubled raises it to 0.121 and switches genre just as often. Picture by picture, the share does not separate the pictures that switched from those that did not.

test value rule verdict
C69 P5 — strong edits lower the style share more than mild ones L06 -0.041, L12 +0.026, L10 -0.020, L19 +0.005 max(strong) < min(mild) not supported
C70 G1 — share lower in switched pictures (20) AUC 0.46 ≥ 0.70 not supported
C70 G1d — share against intensity (20) Spearman +0.05 ≤ -0.40 not supported

Not a text-like push

The second explanation: the edit moves the conditioning the way the words "anime style" would. C71 encoded the five orders with "realistic western comics style" replaced by "anime style", "cartoon style" or "oil painting style", and compared the direction of each swap with the push of each edit. Nothing lines up: every cosine is between -0.12 and +0.07. The three edits that send every order to anime point, if anywhere, slightly away from it. The pushes are 5 to 24 times larger than the word swap (exploratory). The only hint of a direction is cartoon: the cartoon-minus-painting cosine follows the number of cartoon pictures (Spearman 0.52, reported, counts of at most 3).

The fallback is anime

C72 asked what the picture becomes when nothing names a style. The elf prompt was rendered in its five word orders at two seeds without "realistic western comics style", "bold ink outlines" and "hatched shadows". Every labelled picture is anime: 9 of 9, against a bar of 7 of 10 fixed before the labels (one picture was not labelled; the result holds whatever it is). With the style words, the same orders and seeds are Western comic in 9 of 9. The empty prompt is not anime (anime, realistic, anime, painting), so this is not the model's global default. It is what this description of a character becomes when the style words are gone.

Random pushes of the same size

C72 then added to the plain conditioning random pushes as large as the real push of three edits, tap by tap, with no weight edited. The edits were L05 (all orders to anime), L06 (orders scattered) and L28 (largest push, stays comic). A gate checked the instrument first: with no push the render is pixel-identical to the plain one, and passing the real edit's conditioning through gives exactly the edit's render. A first version of the gate, built on stored float16 encodes, failed and was replaced before any other render (amendment 1).

push genre switches (27 labelled cells) ratio to the real edits rule
real edits 14 — —
random, permuted channels 11 0.79 size alone suffices
random, one vector for all tokens 0 0.00 the direction matters
random, noise per token 10 0.71 size alone suffices

By the rule fixed before the labels (amendment 2), the variants disagree, so the answer is "depends on the form of the push". Random pushes that vary from token to token reach the fallback, mostly anime (15 of 21 switches); a shift shared by every token, as large, does nothing to the genre. Edit by edit, the real pushes are not like random ones. L28's random pushes switch 16 of 18 pictures, yet the real L28 edit keeps all 9 a Western comic. L05's random pushes switch 1 of 18, yet the real L05 edit turns all 9 anime.

So size alone does not decide where a strong edit goes; each edit's direction does, and why each points where it does is not known. One untested reason a shared shift may be harmless: the image model's text path normalises what it receives, which could absorb an offset common to every token.

Every character has its own fallback

C73 repeated the no-style test on the seven portraits of page 28 and C65, removing only "Western comics style" from their frame, at four seeds. With the clause all 28 pictures are Western comic; without it, the same faces and costumes come back as paintings or realistic renders, and only one picture of 28 is anime. The fallback depends on the character (pre-registered H1, supported).

Do the edits lead each character to that fallback? No (H2, not supported): switched pictures land on the character's own fallback 0.28 of the time, as often as chance (0.27). What they show instead is a destination per edit, across characters: L06 MLP doubled gives realistic renders, L14 cartoons, L26 and L28 leave the comic alone, others spread. Elves bend several edits toward anime: the elf rogue, whose own fallback is painting, switches to anime in 10 of its 12 switched pictures.

What each phrase draws alone

The same pass rendered each of the 36 phrases of the elf prompt alone, plus a few words, at four seeds. Described, not tested: * "female dwarf" is drawn as a woman with a beard in 4 of 4, and so is the full dwarf prompt. The beard that appears on the dwarf under edits is the model's own picture of a dwarf, not something the edit invents. * "uniform" is an anime girl in a school uniform in 4 of 4. * "realistic western comics style" alone draws bearded cowboys in comic panels: the model reads "western" as the genre of the American West. * The elf's description ("female antlered elf brawler") is anime in 3 of 4. * Phrases without a person are mostly drawn as realistic photographs (78 of 165 labelled single-phrase pictures).

A dose ladder

C74 rendered three MLP edits at twelve doses (0.10 to 1.00) on three portraits at two seeds: L06 (to realistic), L14 (to cartoon) and L28 (keeps the comic, the control). The full-dose render was re-made first and is pixel-identical to the C65 one. For each strip I answered, side by side, where the style starts to differ, whether it moves gradually or in a step, whether the intermediate pictures head toward the full-dose one, where the picture loses coherence and where it loses a trait the prompt asks for. Before labelling I fixed the definitions (amendment 2): a hybrid that reads as one intended style, such as comic lines with painted textures, is a change of style, not a loss of coherence.

test (L06 and L14, 11 changing strips) value rule verdict
H1 — gradual rather than a step 8 of 11 = 0.73 ≥ 0.6 gradual* (pooled)
H2 — intermediate doses head toward the full dose 10 of 11 = 0.91 ≥ 0.7 supported
H3 — style changes before coherence is lost 11 of 11 ≥ 2/3 supported

*The pooled H1 hides two behaviours. L14 slides toward cartoon in 6 of 6 strips. L06 jumps from comic to photograph around 0.80 in 4 of 5. And H3 is met in the simplest way: I marked no loss of coherence anywhere.

What the ladder shows beyond the tests (reported, not tested):

  • The style holds for most of the range. No strip changes style below 0.70. Since the edit scales three matrices of the MLP, the layer's output at 0.70 is, by my estimate of (1 + d)³, already several times the original.
  • The character goes first. In my free-text notes, a trait was lost before the style changed in 5 of 10 L06/L14 strips and at the same dose in 2. Those notes mixed traits the prompt asks for with features it does not name, and were not blind; C75 measured this properly (next section).
  • Composition moves smoothly. In all 18 strips pose and framing change little from one dose to the next, even where the style jumps.

What the edit costs the character

C75 turned the C74 notes into a blind test. Every phrase of the three prompts became a yes/no question ("Is the hair copper-coloured?", "Are there lower tusks jutting past the lips?"), two common ones were added (frontal close-up, white background), and two questions compare with the original: is the skin the same colour, and could it be the same character drawn by another artist. The page asks one question over every picture of a character, shows no dose, edit or seed, and repeats some pictures to measure consistency.

Part A (my labels, the 222 pictures of the C74 ladder). Retention, the share of the original's traits still present, falls with dose under L06 and L14 and barely moves under L28.

test (pre-registered) value rule verdict
T1 — retention falls with dose median Spearman -0.89, 18 strips ≤ -0.50 supported
T2 — traits go before the style (L06, L14) 11 of 11 strips ≥ 2/3 supported
T3 — L28 costs traits without changing style -0.07 ≤ -0.15 inconclusive
T4 — skin changes go lighter 52 of 53 ≥ 0.80, 2 of 3 characters supported
reliability on repeats kappa 0.93 ≥ 0.60 passed

T2 compares a blind measure made of many questions with a single style judgement made without blinding, so it leans toward the traits by construction. With a stricter onset (about two traits lost), traits still go first in 8 of 11 strips, style first in 1 (exploratory).

What goes first are expressions and judgements of degree (the elf's smirk, androgyny, the dwarf's age), then race and costume: the half-orc stops reading as a half-orc at 0.60, then loses her knot, undercut and collar; the dwarf loses her braids and her armour. The elf's pointed ears are never lost.

Part B2, the control. A second labeller, who had seen none of these pictures and did not know what the study is about, labelled the real edits at 0.70, 0.85 and 1.00 next to random pushes of the same size (C72's node, token and permuted variants), plus the unedited portraits at eight seeds.

test (pre-registered) value rule verdict
B1 — random minus real retention, 36 matched cells +0.18 (token +0.20, permuted +0.17) ≥ +0.15, both variants alike the edit costs more than its size
reliability on her repeats kappa 0.98 ≥ 0.60 passed
agreement with my labels, shared pictures kappa 0.85 reported —

The pooled verdict is carried by L06 and L14. L28 goes the other way: its real edit keeps the character better than random pushes of its size, as it kept the comic in C72. So the cost is a property of each edit's direction. Under the real edits, skin changes go lighter in 14 of 14; random pushes change the skin in 6 of 108 pictures. The unedited model never draws five asked traits at any of eight seeds (the dwarf's scars, the half-orc's tusks, dirt and snarl); leaving them out changes no verdict. The two labellers disagree most on whether the dwarf "reads as a dwarf" (8 of 14).

Layer 0 switched off

C77 replicated a page of the C64 pilot notes: with the MLP of layer 0 switched off, the elf came out as text. I switched off the attention or the MLP of layer 0 on three new prompts at the same seed, after re-rendering the C64 elf (pixel-identical). The rule, fixed before the renders, asked for readable text in at least 5 of 6 pictures: it got 4.

prompt (seed 1618033) attention off MLP off whole layer off (exploratory)
elf, comic (C64) text text noise
dwarf, comic text tiled pattern noise
dragonborn, comic text tiled pattern noise
dwarf, watercolour text text over a face noise

On the encoder side (data/te_layer0_encoder_summary.csv), with half the layer off the conditioning keeps a normal size (0.98x and 0.84x on average over the twelve readings) and the identity of each token (a logit lens recovers it in 52 % and 62 % of positions, 51 % unedited). With the whole layer off its size is 21.7x on average, 62x at L05, and no token is recovered. My reading, not tested: the picture writes the prompt when the conditioning keeps the words at a normal size but has lost part of what layer 0 adds to them. No experiment varies the two separately.

There is a precedent on a different encoder. In Stable Diffusion 1.x, causal tracing places the CLIP text encoder's knowledge of styles, objects and facts in its first self-attention layer, at the last token of the subject, and a closed-form edit of that layer removes a concept (README, ref. 31). The same authors found that this localisation does not carry over to SD-XL or DeepFloyd (ref. 20). Here, switching off the attention of Qwen3-VL's first layer is the condition that writes text in 4 of 4 prompts. Whether this is the same property of first layers, on a 4-billion-parameter language model instead of CLIP, is not tested.

Punctuation, BREAK and labels

C78 asked whether the separators between the parts of a prompt matter, on two prompts with four characters each (a prison break and a totem), eight seeds, seven versions. Before the pilot I fixed twelve yes/no questions per prompt; I answered them blind to version and seed (data/te_punct_alessandro.csv, 2,640 answers, repeats kappa 0.954).

version errors per picture against the original better / worse / tied (16 pairs) verdict
original 1.50
commas 1.44 -0.06 5 / 4 / 7 no difference
periods 1.31 -0.19 4 / 1 / 11 no difference
semicolons 1.31 -0.19 6 / 3 / 7 no difference
no punctuation 1.75 +0.25 2 / 6 / 8 no difference
no "Character N" labels 1.69 +0.19 1 / 3 / 12 no difference
BREAK 7.00 +5.50 0 / 16 / 0 worse

With BREAK no picture has all four characters, and the catfolk is never humanoid. The errors left in the other versions are omissions the model makes in every version (the elf's blue sparks: 0 of 8 everywhere). Questions chosen after the pilot, which decide nothing, show one more thing: without the labels two leaks between characters disappear (the orc's green on the elf's fist, the orc's folded arms on the tiefling), but the totem's catfolk becomes an ordinary cat in 7 of 8. On the encoder side, the separator changes how alike the tokens of one part are by less than 0.001 (data/te_punct_encoder_summary.csv).

Inside the text encoder

A probe that only reads (no picture), on 16 prompts, measures how much each of the 36 layers writes into the encoder's internal signal, relative to the size of the signal it receives (data/te_residual_probe_summary.csv).

layers size of the signal after the layer what the layer writes, relative to what it receives
0 12.6 → 106.9 8.5
1-5 186 → 398 0.47-1.23
6 398 → 13,107 33.8 (almost all of it from the MLP)
7-33 13,108 → 14,136 0.012-0.080
34-35 12,768, then 6,606 0.24, 0.65

Described, not tested. L06 doubled is the edit that turned the portraits into realistic renders (11 of 14 in C73) and jumped from comic to photograph in the dose ladder (C74). Whether it is destructive because it writes so much is the next question on the roadmap.

Which taps carry the damage

The image model reads twelve taps of the text encoder: the internal signal entering layers 2, 5, 8, …, 35 (txtfusion normalises them and mixes them before the image model sees them). An edit to layer 6 changes taps 2-11; an edit to layer 14 changes taps 5-11; L28, the edit that keeps the comic and the character, changes only taps 9-11. So: does the damage of L06 and L14 travel through the early and middle taps (0-8), or through the late ones (9-11), where L28 is harmless?

C79 computed the edit's push on the conditioning and let it through only on some taps: the next two (L06) or the next one (L14), the early and middle ones, the late ones. Kept on all twelve, the push reproduces the full edit pixel for pixel; the two halves add up to it exactly. Three characters, four seeds, 72 renders, 108 showings labelled blind with C75's questions, one at a time (data/te_tap_alessandro.csv).

test (pre-registered) value rule verdict
1 — early and middle taps cost more traits than late ones 0.212 against 0.066, +0.146; 5 of 6 pairs ≥ +0.15 and 5 of 6 inconclusive
2 — the taps right after the layer are enough, L06 0.014 / 0.296 = 0.05 ≥ 0.70 enough, ≤ 0.30 not not enough
2 — the same, L14 (one tap) 0.000 / 0.128 = 0.00 same not enough
3 — automatic distances agree (DINOv2 / CSD) 15 of 24 / 3 of 24 cells ≥ 18 of 24 no / opposite
reliability on repeats kappa 1.00 ≥ 0.60 passed

Trait loss on the two seeds where the full edit exists:

edit next taps early and middle late the two halves summed full edit
L06 0.01 0.31 0.07 0.37 0.46
L14 0.00 0.12 0.03 0.16 0.38

Reported, not tested: under L14 the full edit lightens the skin in 4 of 6 pictures and changes the person in 6 of 6, the half-tap pictures in 0 of 24. Under L06 the early and middle taps lighten it in 6 of 12 and change the person in 6 of 12, the late ones in 4 of 12 and 1 of 12. By CSD the late taps move the pictures more (21 of 24 cells); under L06, DINOv2 and VQAScore move more with the early ones: a hint that the late taps carry rendering and the early ones content, from a measure (CSD) that C66 did not validate for style.

Diffusion Lens, which renders images from the intermediate layers of text encoders, finds simple and common concepts early and relations, colour bindings and rare concepts late, built gradually in a T5 encoder (README, ref. 21). The C79 result, damage that needs many readings at once and halves that fall short of the whole, fits a gradual build-up better than a single locus. C87 tests it tap by tap.

Reproducing this

model:
  checkpoint: krea2_turbo_bf16.safetensors
  weight_dtype: default
  sha256: not recorded — the file is outside the repository
sampling:
  sampler: euler_ancestral
  steps: 9
  cfg: 1.0
  denoise: 1.0
  scheduler: simple
  resolution: 1024x1280
  vae: qwen_image_vae.safetensors
  text_encoder: qwen3vl_4b_bf16.safetensors (CLIPLoader type krea2)
tuner:
  node: ArthemyKrea2CLIPTuner
  version: not recorded — the tuner is a separate repository
  mode: Real Value; one layer half through granular_json (layers.L.self_attn.{q,k,v,o}_proj.weight or layers.L.mlp.{gate,up,down}_proj.weight), weight x (1 + d)
prompts:
  files: [data/te_pilot_plan.csv, data/te_characters_plan.csv, data/te_bridge_plan.csv, data/te_default_plan.csv, data/te_fallback_plan.csv, data/te_dose_plan.csv, data/te_traits_plan.csv, data/te_layer0_plan.csv, data/te_punct_plan.csv, data/te_punct2_plan.csv, data/te_punct_nopunct_plan.csv, data/te_tap_isolation_plan.csv]
  ids: [P1_elfbrawler, V1_Original, V2_SubjectFirst, V3_BGFirst, V4_ActionFirst, V5_Inverse, D1_dwarf_paladin, D1W_dwarf_paladin_watercolor, E2_elf_rogue, G5_gnome_wizard, H3_halfling_druid, O4_halforc_fighter, R6_dragonborn_cleric, T7_tiefling_bard, "V1-V5 without the style clauses (C72)", EMPTY, W00-W42 (C72 single phrases), "the seven portraits without 'Western comics style' (C73)"]
seeds: [1618033, 1234567, 2645751, 3141592, 3316624, 2718281, 3605551, 4123105]
conditions:
  - name: one layer half of the text encoder, d = -1.00 (zeroed) or +1.00 (doubled); C64 also at ±0.10 and ±0.35
    dose: 1.000
    measured_D: not measured; the dose is a per-matrix gain, not a calibrated displacement
  - name: C74 dose ladder, MLP of L06, L14, L28 at d = 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 1.00
    dose: 0.10-1.00
    measured_D: not measured; the dose is a per-matrix gain, not a calibrated displacement
  - name: C77 layer 0 attention, MLP or all seven matrices x 0
    dose: -1.00
    measured_D: not measured
  - name: C79 push of L06 or L14 MLP doubled, restricted to taps (2,3 or 4,5), 0-8 or 9-11 (Krea2ConditioningPush, variant taps)
    dose: 1.000
    measured_D: per-tap push norms in data/te_tap_isolation_encoder_by_tap.csv
